Musk Says AT&T and Verizon May "Lose Some Revenue" as Starlink's Phone Service Gets 40x the Bandwidth ©NASA/Kim Shiflett and SUMALI IBNU CHAMID from Alemedia.id via Canva
Key Takeaways

Elon Musk said SpaceX's next direct-to-cell satellites, launching in 2027, will have 40x the bandwidth, and AT&T and Verizon may lose some revenue.

The hit looks small for now, since satellite signals struggle to reach phones indoors, but SpaceX's planned rooftop micro cell towers aim at that gap.

Wireless made 96.9% of AT&T's segment operating income in 2025, so pricing is what a fourth competitor would test.

AST SpaceMobile, the carriers' satellite partner, has the most to prove, and T-Mobile's partner could turn rival.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) wants to sell phone service, and Elon Musk just said out loud what that means for AT&T (T:NYSE) and Verizon (VZ:NYSE). It also lands on AST SpaceMobile (ASTS:NASDAQ), the carriers' satellite partner, and T-Mobile (TMUS:NASDAQ), which sells Starlink's direct-to-cell service as T-Satellite.

At the New York Times DealBook Summit on Nov. 18, Andrew Ross Sorkin asked whether SpaceX would end up buying an American telecom company. Musk laid out his plan instead, said he doesn't expect the carriers to "go out of business or anything," then added: "maybe they'll lose some revenue here."

Some revenue. Noted.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on AT&T, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See AT&T's Analyst Ratings

Texting is just the start

Today's direct-to-cell is a dead-zone product. Starlink said on Nov. 18 that its phone service is now live in Mongolia, where carrier Mobicom offers texting and a short list of apps outside cell coverage. Nobody cancels a phone plan over that.

But Musk said SpaceX starts launching its version 2 constellation next year, which will "have 40 times the bandwidth of the current direct-to-cell version one." That's down from the "more than 100 times" he claimed on X in October. It's still a big jump from a texting service.

Then he named the place satellites struggle to reach: "if you're indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space." His fix is a micro cell tower that sits on a roof like a Starlink dish, going into production "I think, next year." It would run on the 800 MHz spectrum SpaceX agreed to buy from Grain Management. The FCC accepted that deal for review on Nov. 10 but hasn't approved it.

AT&T CEO John Stankey said on the company's third-quarter call that 40% to 45% of its Chicago traffic comes from indoors. He added that AT&T runs six to eight carriers of low-band spectrum per metro, against one for SpaceX.

Blank National Training Center.

The combination of disciplined execution on core wireless and fiber metrics, together with targeted brand and connectivity investments such as the U.S. Soccer partnership, highlights how AT&T is trying to link network scale, customer engagement and long term service relationships rather than relying mainly on one off promotions.

We will now look at how AT&T's clean quarterly execution and record fiber net adds could influence its longer term investment narrative.

Scan beyond AT&T and line up other telecoms and infrastructure plays that could be setting up for the next move with our curated 42 high quality undervalued stocks screener list.

AT&T Investment Narrative Recap

To own AT&T, you need to believe its heavy fiber and 5G spending, plus copper shutdown plans, translate into steadier service revenue and cleaner margins. The analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St focuses on that execution rather than on rapid top line growth. The renewed U.S. Soccer sponsorship and a clean quarter support the brand and indicate disciplined delivery, but they do not meaningfully change this thesis.

The near term swing factor still appears to be progress on cost reductions from legacy copper and the balance between customer incentives and free cash flow. The key risk remains that expenses tied to older networks and device subsidies stay elevated for longer, which could keep profitability and sentiment under pressure even if subscriber trends remain solid.

The renewed multiyear U.S. Soccer partnership is the clearest operational connection to AT&T's current catalyst story. Management is trying to deepen wireless and fiber relationships, and this agreement ties directly into fan engagement, athlete storytelling and the new Arthur M. Blank National Training Center, where AT&T provides advanced connectivity.

For investors, this matters only if sponsorships help support stickier accounts around a converged fiber plus wireless offering that analysts already highlight as important. The risk is that marketing and sponsorship spending increases while copper retirement, cost savings and margin repair advance more slowly, which would leave the business carrying legacy costs without sufficient incremental high quality service revenue.

title: AST SpaceMobile vs. Redwire: Which Space Infrastructure Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

AST SpaceMobile vs. Redwire: Which Space Infrastructure Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool

RDW
T

Trading disclosure

The private space economy is rapidly expanding as satellite technology and infrastructure become more accessible. Deciding between AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ:ASTS) and Redwire (NYSE:RDW) depends on your appetite for high-stakes disruption versus established hardware manufacturing.

AST SpaceMobile seeks to eliminate global connectivity gaps by providing cellular service from orbit. Redwire serves as a critical supplier of components, sensors, and microgravity research platforms. This comparison examines how their differing business models, financial health, and operational risks align with long-term investment goals.

The case for AST SpaceMobile

As a unique entrant among communication stocks, AST SpaceMobile is developing a satellite constellation to deliver broadband directly to mobile devices. It has formed strategic agreements with major carriers including AT&T (NYSE:T) and Verizon Communications (NYSE:VZ) to serve their existing customers. Reliance on these large network operators to reach subscribers introduces a level of customer concentration risk to the business model.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached around $142.9 million. This represents a substantial revenue growth of roughly 671% compared to the prior twelve-month period as the company began its commercial rollout. However, the company still reported a significant net loss of approximately $628.3 million during this same time frame.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio stands at nearly 16.4x. This ratio measures liquid assets against short-term debts, indicating a strong immediate liquidity position. The company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 1.2x, meaning its total liabilities are 1.2 times its shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was negative $1.1 billion.

The case for Redwire

Redwire functions as a diversified infrastructure provider for the aerospace and defense sectors. It supplies essential hardware, such as avionics and power systems, to NASA and various branches of the U.S. military. Beyond government contracts, the company has established commercial partnerships with leaders like Eli Lilly & Co. (NYSE:LLY) to conduct advanced microgravity research in orbit.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $431.9 million. This performance reflects revenue growth of about 45.8% over the previous twelve-month period. Despite the increase in sales, Redwire recorded a net loss of roughly $226.1 million during this cycle as it continues to scale its manufacturing capabilities.

title: Why Is AT&T (T) Down 3.9% Since Last Earnings Report?
detail:
Why Is AT&T (T) Down 3.9% Since Last Earnings Report?
Zacks Equity Research
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 9:30 AM CST 5 min read
T
^GSPC
Trade AT&T on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It has been about a month since the last earnings report for AT&T (T). Shares have lost about 3.9% in that time frame, outperforming the S&P 500.

But investors have to be wondering, will the recent negative trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is AT&T due for a breakout? Well, first let's take a quick look at the latest earnings report in order to get a better handle on the recent drivers for AT&T Inc. before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late.

T Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on Fiber and Wireless Growth

AT&T reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of 65 cents per share, up 20.4% year over year, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of 61 cents by 6.56%. Revenues rose 5.3% to $32.32 billion, beating the $31.68 billion consensus by 2.02%.

Growth in fiber and wireless services supported results, with Advanced Connectivity adding a record 769,000 internet connections. The company also added 379,000 postpaid phone subscribers and raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook.

T's Advanced Connectivity Revenues Gain Ground

Advanced Connectivity revenues increased 7.2% year over year to $29.48 billion. Service revenues rose 6.1% to $23.9 billion, while equipment revenues climbed 12.2% to $5.58 billion, benefiting from stronger wireless equipment activity.

Wireless service revenues rose 5% to $17.76 billion, supported by retail subscriber growth, converged accounts and pricing actions. Promotional discounts partially offset these gains. Advanced home internet revenues jumped 23.4% to $2.98 billion, reflecting fiber and AT&T Internet Air growth, including contributions from the acquired Lumen mass-market fiber business.

AT&T's Internet Additions Reach a Record

The company added 442,000 fiber and 327,000 fixed wireless internet connections during the quarter. Total consumer and business locations reached with fiber exceeded 39 million, keeping AT&T on track to surpass 40 million by year-end.

The advanced home Internet convergence rate reached 42.8%, representing the proportion of advanced home internet customers also subscribing to AT&T's postpaid wireless service. Its converged customer base expanded by approximately 350,000. Postpaid phone churn was 0.92%, indicating the share of subscribers leaving the service.

T's Business Connectivity Growth Offsets Declines

Business fiber and advanced connectivity revenues grew 8.7% year over year to $1.99 billion, primarily on higher fiber and fixed wireless revenues. This contributed to a 2.5% increase in overall business service revenues.

Business transitional and other revenues fell 14.6% to $1.02 billion as demand for virtual private network and wholesale services declined. Other service revenues were down 8.6% to $148 million, illustrating the continuing shift away from older offerings.

title: Is Verizon Stock Worth Buying as Cash Flow Improves but Risks Persist?

Is Verizon Stock Worth Buying as Cash Flow Improves but Risks Persist?

Trading disclosure

Verizon Communications Inc. VZ enters the final quarter of 2026 with better customer trends, higher cash generation and wider margins. Management has also raised its earnings, subscriber and free cash flow outlooks.

Those gains improve the investment case, but they do not remove the main constraints. Lower revenue per account, heavy network spending and elevated debt keep the risk-reward profile balanced.

Verizon's Cash Flow Strengthens the Bull Case

Free cash flow rose 14.3% year over year to $18.01 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Verizon now expects full-year free cash flow of $22.44-$22.54 billion, up from its prior $21.94-$22.14 billion forecast.

The stronger cash base supports dividends, debt reduction and share repurchases. Verizon returned $12.8 billion to shareholders in the first nine months, including $4 billion of buybacks, and still expects up to $4.5 billion of repurchases for 2026.

VZ's Valuation Leaves Room for Selective Optimism

Verizon trades at 8.65X forward 12-month earnings, close to its five-year median of 8.73X. Its forward price-to-sales multiple of 1.33X is also near the five-year median of 1.28X, suggesting the shares are not pricing in an aggressive growth outlook.

The stock's Value Score of A adds support to the valuation argument. Still, a favorable value profile works best alongside stronger earnings revisions and operating momentum, so valuation alone is not enough to settle the case.

Verizon's Growth Still Faces Pricing Pressure

Third-quarter postpaid phone net additions reached 406,000, while postpaid phone churn improved four basis points to 0.94%. Verizon raised its 2026 postpaid phone net-addition outlook to 1.1-1.2 million.

Monetization remains a pressure point. Postpaid average service revenue per account fell 1.9% year over year to $168.08. AT&T Inc. T added 379,000 postpaid phones in the third quarter, underscoring continued competition for wireless customers. T-Mobile US, Inc. TMUS reported 274,000 postpaid net account additions and 4% growth in postpaid average revenue per account, showing that rivals are still pressing both subscriber growth and account economics.

VZ's Debt and Capital Needs Limit Flexibility

Total debt stood at $166.23 billion at Sept. 30, 2026, up from $158.15 billion at year-end 2025. Interest expense increased 19% in the first nine months to $5.88 billion, while $23.89 billion of debt was due within one year.

Capital demands also remain substantial. Verizon spent $11.93 billion on capital expenditures in the first nine months and continues to expect $16-$16.5 billion for 2026 as it funds fiber, spectrum, network upgrades and AI Connect investments.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

AT&T (T) shares lost 10.6% over the past year, dividends included, while the S&P 500 gained 9.7%. Many investors still think of AT&T as a traditional phone company saddled with old copper lines. The telecom giant, however, may be building a business that the share price has not yet caught up with, expanding one home at a time. What is AT&T building, and is it working yet?

AT&T shares lost 10.6% in a year when the S&P 500 rose. If AT&T is a big part of your savings, another year like that would hurt. Selling shares bought years ago at lower prices could also cost you in taxes. In a free 30-minute review, our partner advisory firm can show you ways to limit your loss if the stock falls further and to sell with a smaller tax bill. Book the free review.

AT&T Is Winning Homes That Take Fiber And Wireless

AT&T is steadily wiring more homes with fiber and bundling those connections with wireless plans under a single account. The company has set a target of 60 million or more fiber locations by the end of the decade. In fiscal Q3 2026, AT&T Fiber added a net 416,000 customers.

AT&T's home internet push, on fiber and its Internet Air service, is already paying off. Management said service revenue from advanced home internet, which covers both, grew more than 23% from a year earlier in that quarter. Nearly 43% of these home internet customers also had an AT&T postpaid wireless account. AT&T added about 350,000 of these combined accounts in the quarter, at a faster pace than in the second quarter.

How Much Is AT&T Growing As A Whole?

AT&T grew its revenue 3.5% over the past year, to $129 billion. At that size, AT&T can lift the total only slowly by adding fiber homes. Nearly all of AT&T's sales come from one segment, Communications, which made up 96.2% of revenue in fiscal 2025. Still, growth picked up in fiscal Q3 2026. Management said service revenue rose 3.8% from a year earlier, its best gain in more than four years. Total revenue rose 5.3% from a year earlier in that quarter.

The current share price appears to assume little of that, though AT&T's heavy debt, covered below, also helps keep it low. AT&T's latest close sits 24.9% below its highest close of the past year, set on March 27, 2026. Buyers pay 11.4 times trailing earnings for the stock, compared with 21.5 for the S&P 500. Measured in cash, each $100 of AT&T stock now comes with about $11.90 of free cash flow over the past year. A lasting pickup in growth from fiber homes could therefore become the upside surprise for this stock.

Key Takeaways

A $350,000 portfolio split evenly across AT&T, ONEOK and T. Rowe Price pays about $17,500 a year in dividends at today's prices.

ONEOK's distributable cash flow covers its dividend 2.25x, and AT&T pays out 44% of its free cash flow, so both checks look well covered.

T. Rowe Price is the least covered, paying out 71% of its free cash flow while clients pull money from its funds, though it holds more cash than debt.

If T. Rowe Price halved its dividend, the income would fall to about $14,600 a year, and to about $11,700 if it stopped paying.

Picture a hypothetical 72-year-old retiree who splits $350,000 evenly across three big dividend payers: AT&T (T:NYSE), ONEOK (OKE:NYSE) and T. Rowe Price Group (TROW:NASDAQ).

At today's prices, that buys about 5,220 shares of AT&T, about 1,320 of ONEOK and about 1,112 of T. Rowe Price. Together, they pay about $17,500 a year, or $1,423 a month. That's a 5.0% yield on this part of the portfolio. (Of course, no one should ever own just three stocks.)

Source: TIKR, at today's prices and each company's current dividend rate.

AT&T has room to spare, but no raise planned

AT&T plans to keep its dividend at $1.11 a share a year while it buys back $24 billion+ of stock through 2028. AT&T paid out 44% of its free cash flow over the twelve months to Sept. 30, and consensus has 46% for fiscal 2026. Its free cash flow has topped its dividends every year since fiscal 2016:

AT&T (T): free cash flow vs. dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

AT&T has cut before. It paid $2.08 a share in fiscal 2020 and $1.11 in fiscal 2025, and since fiscal 2023 the payout has run between 39.8% and 44.3% of free cash flow.

Fiber is replacing copper inside the business. Third-quarter revenue rose 5.3% from a year before to $32.3 billion, while Legacy revenue fell 24.5% as AT&T shuts its copper network down. CEO John Stankey said on the third-quarter call that "the most durable customer combination in our industry is a fiber-fed broadband customer with a great wireless service on top of it, bar none."

Debt is the risk. Net debt is 3.27x EBITDA on TIKR's figures after AT&T bought spectrum from EchoStar, and the company doesn't expect to reach its 2.5x target until 2029.
